study.title: Revelation 12 The dragon, the woman, and the perseverance of the saints
study.overview: Revelation 12 portrays, through symbolic signs, the conflict between God and the enemy around the people of God and the testimony of Jesus. The central scene is not only the struggle of a dragon against a woman, but the certainty that Satan has already been defeated in the decisive plane and now acts with anger because he knows that there is little time left. The chapter connects the birth of the Son, God's protection of his people in the wilderness, the expulsion of the accuser and the final persecution against those who remain faithful. The practical message is of resistance: the saints win by the blood of the Lamb, by witness and faithfulness to the end.

outline.title: Woman, the Son and the Preservation in the Desert
outline.explanation: John sees a glorious woman, in labor pains, persecuted by a dragon. The Son is born, is destined to rule the nations and is taken to God, while the woman receives a place prepared and sustenance in the desert for a limited period. The picture points to the protective action of God in the midst of the opposition of evil.

outline.title: The war in the sky and the fall of the accuser
outline.explanation: Michael and his angels fight the dragon, who is identified as the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan. He loses his place in heaven and is thrown to earth. The heavenly voice interprets the event as the arrival of salvation and the kingdom of God, and states that the brethren overcome by the blood of the Lamb, by witness and faithfulness to death.

outline.title: Persecution on earth and war against the rest of the offspring
outline.explanation: Expulsion from the sky, the dragon chases the woman, but she is preserved in a providential manner. The earth helps the woman, frustrating the symbolic attack of the serpent. Frustrated, the dragon turns his wrath against the rest of her offspring: those who keep the commandments of God and keep the testimony of Jesus Christ.

study.context: The chapter presents a symbolic reading of the history of redemption and spiritual conflict. The study notes highlight that the woman represents the people of God; in Tyndale, she portrays the people of God and the church under attack, even though the evil one has already been defeated in his main attempt. Matthew Henry understands the scene as a recap of the conflict between the woman's offspring and that of the serpent, echoing Genesis 3:15. Adam Clarke also sees the woman as the true church of Christ. The text uses images of the Old Testament to show protection, desert, childbirth, and battle, without requiring every detail to be read literally.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter states three central truths. First, Christ is the center of victory: the Son destined to rule the nations has already been exalted to God, and the accuser can no longer hold his position before the throne. Second, the suffering of God's people does not mean abandonment, but preservation in the midst of the test; the desert is a place of divine care, even though not of the absence of tribulation. Third, spiritual warfare is real, but their outcome is already decided: the saints win not by self-force, but by the blood of the Lamb, by public witness and perseverance to death. The chapter also shows that Christian fidelity provokes opposition from the world and evil, but this opposition is limited and temporary. The identity of God's people is marked by obedience and testimony of Jesus.

scholarViews.insight: The woman symbolizes the people of God, and the vision summarizes the devil's attack throughout history, despite his decisive defeat; the chapter is divided between the scene of conflict, war in heaven and war on earth.
The vision resumes the enmity announced between the offspring of the woman and that of the serpent, showing the struggle between the church and the antichrist as part of God's revealed purpose.
The woman represents the true church of Christ; childbirth and persecution symbolize the violence suffered by the Christian community in the face of enemy power.

questions: In what ways does the image of the woman in the desert help to understand the protection of God without denying the reality of suffering?
How do the claim that the saints win through the blood of the Lamb and by the testimony confronts our idea of victory?
In what concrete situations today do those who keep God's commandments and have the testimony of Jesus experience opposition similar to that described in this chapter?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to perseverance. When the opposition seems strong, remember that the defeat of the accuser has already been declared and that the preservation of God does not fail. Practice three attitudes: maintain visible obedience to God's commandments, speak of Christ with fidelity even under pressure and accept that Christian victory can go through suffering without losing hope. In concrete terms, choose an area in which you have given up to fear or discouragement and turn it into daily prayer, clear witness and practical obedience.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided present different interpretive readings and, in part, related to specific historical contexts that cannot be treated here as certain facts of the text. Tyndale's passage to verse 1 is incomplete in the quotation provided, but the central idea of the woman as God's people was preserved. The chapter is highly symbolic, so some detailed applications remain open to more than one responsible evangelical reading.
